Patient Vignette: "Priya"

Priya is a 32-year-old single South Asian woman who works as a registered nurse in a busy urban emergency department. She presents for therapy at the urging of her nursing supervisor, who has noticed a sharp decline in her performance over the past eight months. She is thin, with dark circles under her eyes that no amount of concealer seems to hide. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped tightly in her lap, and speaks in a low, measured voice, as if afraid of being overheard.

The event that changed everything happened on a cool October evening. Priya was working a double shift when a mass casualty event was announced: a multi-vehicle collision on the highway involving a bus carrying schoolchildren. The ED became a blur of sirens, gurneys, and screaming. Priya was assigned to a nine-year-old boy, his small body broken and bleeding. She remembers the way his hand felt in hers—so small, so cold—as she held a pressure dressing to his chest. She remembers the doctor’s voice, calm and clinical, calling out vitals that were slipping away. She remembers the exact moment his grip went slack, and the flat line on the monitor. She remembers the mother arriving, her wail cutting through the noise of the department like a knife. Priya had seen death before, many times. But this was different. This was a child. And she was the last person to hold his hand.

In the weeks that followed, Priya could not stop seeing the boy’s face. She would be in the grocery store, reaching for a box of cereal, and she would see him. She would be driving home from work and see his small hand reaching out from the back seat of the car in front of her. She began to avoid the pediatric wing entirely, trading shifts with colleagues, making excuses. At first, it was just the children. Then it became anyone with a chest wound. Then it became the sound of sirens on her day off, which would send her heart racing and her palms slick with sweat. She started driving home the long way, a twenty-minute detour to avoid the intersection where the accident had occurred, even though the accident had happened miles away.

Her sleep unraveled. She would jolt awake at 3:17 a.m.—the exact time the boy had coded—drenched in sweat, gasping for air. Some nights, she would stay awake, sitting on the floor of her bathroom with the light on, because the darkness felt too much like the inside of the ambulance bay. She stopped answering calls from her mother, who lives in Mumbai and worries. She stopped going to temple with her aunt. She stopped cooking, the smell of turmeric and cumin now making her nauseous—it reminded her of the antiseptic and blood that had mixed in the trauma bay.

At work, she is a ghost of her former self. She is meticulous, almost obsessively so, checking IV lines three times, re-counting sponges, re-checking labels. Her colleagues think she is being careful. In truth, she is terrified of making a mistake, of being responsible for another death. She has become hypervigilant, flinching at the sound of a dropped tray, scanning every waiting room for a mother in distress. Her supervisor has had to pull her aside twice for crying in the supply closet after a code. Priya tells her it’s just stress. She knows it is more.

She has not told anyone the full story. Not her colleagues, who were there. Not her mother, who would only worry. Not her friends, who she has stopped seeing. The guilt is a physical weight in her chest. She replays the code in her head every day, wondering if she could have done something differently—if she had pressed harder, if she had called for help sooner, if she had just been faster. She knows, intellectually, that the boy was too injured to survive. But knowing and feeling are two different things.

Now, sitting in this office, she tells me she is tired. She is tired of the nightmares, tired of the jumpiness, tired of the way her heart pounds when a phone rings unexpectedly. She is tired of being afraid. She wants to go back to being the nurse who could handle anything, the one who was steady and strong. But she doesn’t know how.
